title: Medicare cost basics
summary: Explains the costs of Medicare, including premiums and cost sharing across Original Medicare, Medicare Advantage, Medigap and Part D, financial help programs, and late enrollment penalties.

atoms.title: Premiums and cost sharing in Medicare
atoms.question: What costs do I pay with Medicare?
atoms.text: Medicare isn't free. The amount you pay depends on the coverage you choose, the services you use during the year, and whether your plan has in-network and out-of-network rules. Medicare Part B and most Part C, Part D and Medigap plans charge monthly premiums, and in some cases there is a Part A premium. A premium is a fixed amount you pay for coverage to Medicare, a private insurance company, or both. You also pay a share of care costs through deductibles, copays and coinsurance.

atoms.title: Deductible, copay and coinsurance defined
atoms.question: What are a deductible, copay and coinsurance?
atoms.text: A deductible is a set amount you pay out of pocket for covered services before Medicare or your plan begins to pay. A copay is a fixed amount you pay at the time you receive a covered service, such as $20 for a doctor visit or $12 for a prescription. Coinsurance is your share of the total cost as a percentage; for example, with 25% coinsurance on a $100 service you would pay $25 and your insurance would pay $75.

atoms.title: Costs of Original Medicare Part A and Part B
atoms.question: How much does Medicare Part A and Part B cost?
atoms.text: With Medicare Part A, most people don't pay a premium, though you may if you or your spouse worked and paid Medicare taxes for less than 10 years. Medicare Part B has a monthly premium you pay directly to Medicare, and the amount can vary based on your income level. Other costs with Part A and Part B include deductibles, coinsurance and copays.

atoms.title: Medicare Advantage costs and out-of-pocket maximum
atoms.question: What are my costs with a Medicare Advantage plan?
atoms.text: Each Medicare Advantage (Part C) plan sets its own specific costs, but the types of costs you may pay include premiums, deductibles, copays and coinsurance. Not all plans will have deductibles, copays or coinsurance, so check each plan's cost-sharing rules carefully. Medicare Advantage plans also limit how much you'll pay out of pocket every year, called the out-of-pocket maximum, and each year the limit is set by Medicare.

atoms.title: Medigap costs and predictability
atoms.question: What are my costs with a Medicare Supplement plan?
atoms.text: Medicare Supplement plans are designed to help limit out-of-pocket costs by helping to pay for some of the costs Original Medicare doesn't pay. There are Medigap plan options available with low to no copays, and the plans offer predictable out-of-pocket costs. Benefits and costs vary depending on the plan you choose. Different plan options are available in Massachusetts, Minnesota and Wisconsin.

atoms.title: 2026 Part D out-of-pocket maximum is $2,100
atoms.question: What is the Part D out-of-pocket maximum for 2026?
atoms.text: Standalone Part D plans (PDP) and Medicare Advantage plans with drug coverage (MAPD) set their own costs, but the types of costs they can include are similar: premiums, deductibles, copays and coinsurance. For 2026, the annual out-of-pocket maximum is $2,100. The amount you pay depends on the drug payment stage you're in and the tier a drug is in, if your plan has a tiered formulary. Part D plan costs can vary widely, even for similar coverage.
questions: What is the Part D out-of-pocket cap in 2026?

Do Part D costs vary between plans?

atoms.title: The three Part D drug payment stages
atoms.question: What are the Part D drug payment stages?
atoms.text: 1) Annual Deductible: for plans with a deductible, you pay the full cost of drugs until you reach it, then move to Initial Coverage; plans without a deductible start at Initial Coverage with your first prescription. 2) Initial Coverage: the plan pays its share and you pay your copay or coinsurance, until total drug costs reach $2,100 in 2026. 3) Catastrophic Coverage: once you or others on your behalf reach $2,100 in out-of-pocket drug costs, you pay $0 for Medicare-covered Part D drugs for the rest of the plan year.

atoms.title: Programs that help pay Medicare costs
atoms.question: What programs can help me pay Medicare costs?
atoms.text: If you have limited income and assets, you may qualify for help with Medicare costs, and many people who could qualify never sign up. Extra Help from Medicare helps pay some or all Part D premiums, deductibles, copays and coinsurance. Medicare savings programs help pay Part A and Part B premiums, deductibles and coinsurance, and qualifying for one automatically qualifies you for Extra Help. Medicaid covers individuals and families with limited incomes and may include services Medicare does not, like prescription drugs, eye care or long-term care.

atoms.title: PACE and state pharmaceutical assistance
atoms.question: What is PACE and what other help programs exist?
atoms.text: Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE) combine medical, social and long-term care services for people over the age of 55 who qualify, and the program is not available in all states. Other programs may be available in your state, such as State Pharmaceutical Assistance Programs. Each program has its own rules for qualifying, so read about each carefully. If you have both Medicaid and Medicare, you may be eligible for a Dual Special Needs plan (D-SNP).

atoms.title: Look beyond premiums when comparing plans
atoms.question: Should I only compare Medicare premiums?
atoms.text: It's easy to focus on just premiums, but it's a better idea to look at all of your Medicare costs together, including premiums and all out-of-pocket costs. A plan may look like a good choice with a low premium but actually cost more with a high deductible or high copayments for doctor visits or prescriptions. The reverse can also be true: a high premium but low out-of-pocket costs. You may reduce costs by understanding cost sharing, using services wisely and adopting healthy lifestyle behaviors.

atoms.title: Medicare late enrollment penalties by part
atoms.question: What are the Medicare late enrollment penalties for Parts A, B and D?
atoms.text: Part A, Part B and Part D may charge premium penalties if you miss your initial enrollment dates, unless you qualify for a Special Enrollment Period. Part A: if you must pay a premium, the late penalty is 10%, charged for twice the number of years you delayed. Part B: an additional 10% for each 12-month period you delay, usually paid every month for as long as you have Part B. Part D: 1% of the average Part D premium for each month you delay, paid for as long as you have Part D.
questions: How much is the Part B late penalty?
How long do I pay the Part A late penalty?
What is the Part D late enrollment penalty?

atoms.title: Part B penalty ends at 65 for disabled enrollees
atoms.question: Does the Part B late penalty ever end?
atoms.text: In most cases, you have to pay the Part B late enrollment penalty every month for as long as you have Part B. However, if you're under 65 and disabled, any Part B penalty ends once you turn 65, because you'll have another Initial Enrollment Period based on your age. For Part A, you won't pay a premium if you or your spouse worked and paid taxes for at least 10 years, and the Part A penalty applies no matter how long you delay enrollment.
